catalog_quote: 2.5 Stress. The stress on a word is usually on the second last syllable. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is regularly penultimate; occasionally antepenultimate; never final in polysyllables. Enclitic suffixes/particles (person markers, na 'when') count in the stress domain and pull stress rightward onto the new penult; the particles ma 'cause' and de 'if' do not shift stress and are treated as separate words.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress 'does sometime occur on the third last syllable' (no conditioning given; example ó-ni-a 'he went' with final vowel sequence); ma 'cause' and de 'if' do not trigger stress shift.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including suffixed particles; Thomson uses stress placement (penult of the whole complex) as the criterion for orthographic word division (sec. 3.2). Impressionistic description by a fluent missionary-doctor speaker, analysed with Dutton and Taylor; based mainly on western Magi (assistant from Loupomu village), with Varo/Boru/Asiaro dialect notes in footnotes.
new_statements.identity_note: Thomson calls the language 'Magi (or Mailu as it is sometimes called)'; same language as Glottolog mail1248 / ISO mgu. Description based chiefly on western Magi (his assistant was from Loupomu village; paradigms labelled 'Magi-West'), with Varo, Boru and Asiaro dialect differences confined to footnotes; the stress statement is given for Magi as a whole.

sources.note: Sec. 2.5 'Stress' (pp.605-606): stress usually on the second-last syllable, sometimes on the third-last, never on the last syllable of a polysyllabic word; examples show enclitic particles (na 'when') shifting stress rightward (o-ni-a 'he went' -> o-ni-a-na), while ma 'cause' and de 'if' do not; sec. 3.21-3.22 (p.607) uses this penultimate-stress behaviour as the criterion for word division; acute accent marks stressed syllable (3.3).
Bibliographic check only; the two descriptive refs (Thomson 1975, Saville 1912) are the ones downloaded above.
